subject: Legal Studies
name: Legal Studies, Year 12
about: HSC, Crime, human rights and options
syllabus: NSW Legal Studies Stage 6 Syllabus (2009), HSC (Year 12) course, Crime, Human rights and the seven options

points.title: What a crime is
points.brief: A crime is an act or omission against society that is forbidden by law and punished by the state.

points.title: Actus reus and mens rea
points.brief: Most crimes need a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea), such as intent or recklessness. The prosecution must prove both.

points.title: Strict and absolute liability
points.brief: For some offences, such as many traffic offences, no guilty mind needs to be proved. Strict liability allows a defence of honest mistake; absolute liability does not.

points.title: Categories of crime
points.brief: Offences against the person, against property, drug offences, public order offences, white collar crime, driving offences and offences against the state.

points.title: Summary and indictable offences
points.brief: Summary offences are minor and heard by a magistrate. Indictable offences are serious and can be tried by a judge and jury.

points.title: Causes of crime
points.brief: Social and economic factors, such as poverty and disadvantage, psychological factors, opportunity and peer pressure can all contribute to crime.

points.title: Police powers
points.brief: Police can stop, search and arrest people, but their powers are set by law, in NSW mainly the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002.

points.title: Gathering evidence and warrants
points.brief: Police gather evidence through searches, interviews and forensic tests. A warrant from a court is needed for many searches and for surveillance.

points.title: Rights of suspects
points.brief: Suspects have rights, such as being told why they are arrested and having access to a lawyer. The right to silence has limits in NSW.

points.title: Bail and remand
points.brief: Bail releases an accused person before trial, with conditions. A person refused bail is held on remand. Bail laws balance the presumption of innocence with community safety.

points.title: The prosecution and defence
points.brief: The prosecution, for the state, must prove the charge. The defence tests the evidence. Both sides have duties to the court.

points.title: The burden and standard of proof
points.brief: The prosecution carries the burden of proof and must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The accused is presumed innocent.

points.title: Pleas and charge negotiation
points.brief: An accused pleads guilty or not guilty. In charge negotiation, the accused pleads guilty to a lesser or fewer charges, which saves time but can seem unfair to victims.

points.title: Juries
points.brief: In serious trials, a jury of 12 decides guilt. NSW allows a majority verdict of 11 to 1 in some cases.

points.title: Defences to criminal charges
points.brief: Complete defences, such as self-defence and duress, lead to acquittal. Partial defences, such as substantial impairment, reduce murder to manslaughter.

points.title: Purposes of punishment
points.brief: Sentences aim at deterrence, retribution, rehabilitation, incapacitation and denunciation, and judges weigh these against each other.

points.title: Aggravating and mitigating factors
points.brief: Aggravating factors, such as violence or a prior record, make a sentence harsher. Mitigating factors, such as remorse or a guilty plea, make it lighter.

points.title: Types of penalties
points.brief: Penalties range from fines and good behaviour orders to community correction orders, intensive correction orders and imprisonment.

points.title: Appeals
points.brief: Either side can appeal against a sentence, and the accused can appeal against a conviction, to a higher court.

points.title: Alternative methods of sentencing
points.brief: Circle sentencing involves Aboriginal elders in sentencing Aboriginal offenders. Restorative justice brings offenders and victims together.

points.title: Post-sentencing
points.brief: Parole lets prisoners serve part of a sentence in the community under supervision. Some serious offenders can be kept in custody or supervised after their sentence ends.

points.title: The age of criminal responsibility
points.brief: In NSW, children under 10 cannot be charged with a crime. For those aged 10 to 13, the prosecution must also prove the child knew the act was seriously wrong (doli incapax).

points.title: The Young Offenders Act 1997
points.brief: The Act lets police deal with young people through warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences instead of court, to keep them out of the system.

points.title: The Children's Court
points.brief: A closed court for young offenders, with a focus on rehabilitation. Young people's names are usually kept private.

points.title: International crime
points.brief: Crimes against international law, such as genocide and war crimes, and transnational crimes, such as drug trafficking and cybercrime, which cross borders.

points.title: Responses to international crime
points.brief: The International Criminal Court tries genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Extradition and police cooperation deal with transnational crime.

points.title: What human rights are
points.brief: Human rights belong to every person because they are human. They are universal, inherent, inalienable and indivisible.

points.title: The development of human rights
points.brief: Ideas of human rights grew through documents such as Magna Carta and the 18th-century declarations of rights, and through campaigns against slavery and for workers' and women's rights.

points.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
points.brief: Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, the UDHR sets out rights for all people. It is not binding itself, but it led to binding treaties.

points.title: Types of rights
points.brief: Civil and political rights, such as free speech; economic, social and cultural rights, such as education; and collective rights, such as self-determination.

points.title: Sovereignty and enforcement
points.brief: Countries are sovereign, so human rights are hard to enforce against a state that will not comply. Pressure comes from the UN, other states, NGOs and the media.

points.title: Rights in the Australian Constitution
points.brief: The Constitution has few express rights, such as trial by jury for Commonwealth indictable offences, and the High Court has found an implied freedom of political communication.

points.title: Statutes that protect rights
points.brief: Laws such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 and the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 protect rights in particular areas.

points.title: The Australian Human Rights Commission
points.brief: The Commission investigates complaints of discrimination, educates the public and reports on human rights.

points.title: The bill of rights debate
points.brief: Supporters say a bill of rights would protect rights better. Opponents say it would hand power from parliament to unelected judges. Victoria, the ACT and Queensland have human rights acts.

points.title: Who is a consumer
points.brief: A consumer buys goods or services for personal or household use. Consumer law protects them because sellers usually hold more power and information.

points.title: Contracts
points.brief: A contract needs an offer, acceptance, consideration and an intention to be legally bound. Some terms are implied by law even if not written.

points.title: The Australian Consumer Law
points.brief: The ACL gives consumer guarantees, such as goods being of acceptable quality, and bans misleading or deceptive conduct and unfair contract terms.

points.title: Remedies for consumers
points.brief: Consumers can ask for a repair, replacement or refund, complain to NSW Fair Trading, or take a claim to NCAT.

points.title: Consumer credit
points.brief: The National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 requires lenders to be licensed and to check that a loan is not unsuitable for the borrower.

points.title: Consumers and online shopping
points.brief: Buying online raises issues of scams, sellers based overseas and data privacy, which the law is still catching up with.

points.title: Marriage
points.brief: The Marriage Act 1961 sets the rules for a valid marriage. Since 2017 it has allowed two people of any sex to marry.

points.title: De facto relationships
points.brief: Couples who live together without marrying have most of the same legal rights when they separate, under the Family Law Act 1975.

points.title: Divorce
points.brief: Australia has no-fault divorce. A couple must show the marriage has broken down, proved by 12 months of separation.

points.title: Children after separation
points.brief: The best interests of the child are the court's first concern in deciding where a child lives and how much time they spend with each parent.

points.title: Domestic violence and the law
points.brief: Apprehended violence orders protect people from violence or harassment. NSW made coercive control in current or former intimate relationships a crime from 2024.

points.title: Surrogacy and birth technologies
points.brief: Altruistic surrogacy is legal in NSW, but paid surrogacy is a crime. The law is still working out the rights of everyone involved.

points.title: The environment as a global issue
points.brief: Pollution, climate change and loss of species cross borders, so no one country can solve them alone.

points.title: International environmental agreements
points.brief: Treaties such as the Paris Agreement on climate change and the Convention on Biological Diversity set shared goals, though most rely on countries keeping their own promises.

points.title: Principles of environmental law
points.brief: Ecologically sustainable development, the precautionary principle and intergenerational equity guide environmental law.

points.title: Australian environmental law
points.brief: The Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 protects matters of national environmental significance, such as world heritage areas and threatened species.

points.title: Courts and NGOs in protecting the environment
points.brief: Courts such as the NSW Land and Environment Court hear environmental cases, and NGOs campaign, take legal action and monitor compliance.

points.title: Indigenous peoples under international law
points.brief: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) sets out rights to culture, land and self-determination. Australia endorsed it in 2009.

points.title: Self-determination
points.brief: The right of Indigenous peoples to make decisions about their own lives, lands and communities.

points.title: Land rights and native title
points.brief: The Mabo decision (1992) recognised native title and rejected terra nullius. The Native Title Act 1993 set out how native title is claimed.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and the justice system
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are imprisoned at far higher rates than other Australians, which reviews and inquiries have tried to address.

points.title: Effectiveness of the law for Indigenous peoples
points.brief: Weighing what the law has achieved, such as native title, against continuing gaps in health, justice and recognition.

points.title: Shelter as a right
points.brief: Adequate housing is a human right in international law, but in Australia there is no legal right to housing.

points.title: Renting
points.brief: The Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) sets the rights and duties of landlords and tenants, such as bonds, repairs and notice periods.

points.title: Buying a home
points.brief: Most people borrow to buy a home through a mortgage, which lets the lender sell the home if repayments are not made.

points.title: Strata and community living
points.brief: Owners of units share the building and its common areas, governed by strata law and the owners corporation's by-laws.

points.title: Homelessness and public housing
points.brief: Governments provide public and social housing for people on low incomes, but waiting lists are long and homelessness is rising.

points.title: The Fair Work Act 2009
points.brief: The main law for workplaces, which sets the National Employment Standards, such as leave entitlements and maximum hours.

points.title: Awards and enterprise agreements
points.brief: Modern awards set minimum pay and conditions for an industry. Enterprise agreements are negotiated in a workplace and must leave workers better off overall.

points.title: Work health and safety
points.brief: Employers have a duty to keep workers safe, under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW). SafeWork NSW enforces it.

points.title: Discrimination and harassment at work
points.brief: It is against the law to treat workers unfairly because of their sex, race, age, disability and other attributes, or to sexually harass them.

points.title: Unfair dismissal
points.brief: A worker sacked in a harsh, unjust or unreasonable way can apply to the Fair Work Commission for reinstatement or compensation.

points.title: What world order means
points.brief: World order is the set of rules, institutions and relationships that keep peace and security between countries.

points.title: The United Nations and the Security Council
points.brief: The UN Charter bans the use of force except in self-defence or when authorised by the Security Council, whose five permanent members can veto decisions.

points.title: Peacekeeping
points.brief: UN peacekeepers help keep peace after conflicts, with the consent of the parties, as in Timor-Leste.

points.title: International humanitarian law
points.brief: The Geneva Conventions set rules for armed conflict, protecting civilians, prisoners of war and the wounded.

points.title: The responsibility to protect
points.brief: The idea that states must protect their people from mass atrocities, and that the international community should act when they fail to.

points.title: International courts
points.brief: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states, and the International Criminal Court tries individuals for the worst crimes.
